dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — At the pharmacy
dialogs.intro: Ani wakes up with a sore throat and a slight fever. Rahim takes her to the pharmacy at the end of the lane. Watch the **-কে** ending, which marks who an action is aimed at.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: Go ahead, what seems to be the problem?

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: My throat hurts. And I have a slight fever.
lines.literal: my — throat — pain — is-doing. and — a-little — fever.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: For how many days? Any cough?

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Two days. No cough, but a runny nose.
lines.literal: two — days. cough — not-there, but — cold — is-there.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: Have you taken your temperature? How high?

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: A hundred degrees. It went up last night.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: I'll give you this medicine. Three times a day.
lines.literal: you-to — this — medicine-the — am-giving. day-in — three-times.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: Take it after meals. Not on an empty stomach.
lines.literal: food-of — after — eat-to — will-be. empty — stomach-on — not.

lines.speaker: ফার্মাসিস্ট:
lines.id: If it doesn't ease in two days, go to the doctor.
lines.literal: two — days-in — not — if-lessens — doctor-of — near-to — will-go.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Thank you. I should drink warm water, right?
lines.literal: thanks. me-to — hot — water — drink-to — will-be, right — not?

notes: **The -কে ending marks who or what an action is aimed at.** আমি **আপনাকে** বলছি (I'm telling you), **ডাক্তারকে** দেখান (show it to the doctor), **তাকে** ডাকুন (call him/her). The pronoun forms: আমি → **আমাকে**, তুমি → **তোমাকে**, আপনি → **আপনাকে**, সে → **তাকে**, আমরা → **আমাদের**, তারা → **তাদের**.

⚠️ **-কে is used almost only for people and living things, not objects.** বইটা দিন (give me the book) — no -কে. আমাকে বইটা দিন (give the book to me) — -কে on the person only. Bengali marks people but leaves objects bare, because people can act and objects usually can't.

**Complaints use the same pattern as Unit 15: the owner comes first, the complaint is the subject.** আমার **মাথা ব্যথা করছে** (I have a headache — literally “of me head pain is doing”), আমার **জ্বর হয়েছে** (I have a fever — “of me fever has happened”), আমার **পেট খারাপ** (my stomach is upset). ⚠️ Don't say *আমি অসুস্থ করছি*; say আমার শরীর খারাপ or আমি অসুস্থ.
**Medicine is “eaten”, not “drunk” or “taken”.** ওষুধ **খাওয়া** is the right and only form — where English says *take medicine*, Bengali says *eat medicine*, even for syrup.

**… তে হবে means “have to”.** আমাকে যেতে হবে (I have to go), ওষুধ খেতে হবে (the medicine has to be taken), আপনাকে বিশ্রাম নিতে হবে (you have to rest). ⚠️ The person takes the **-কে** ending, not the subject form — so *আমি যেতে হবে* is wrong; say **আমাকে যেতে হবে**. Literally “to me going will be”.

⚠️ **মুখ means both face and mouth**, and context decides. মুখ ধোয়া is washing your face; মুখ খোলা is opening your mouth. Likewise **পেট** is both belly and stomach: পেট ব্যথা (stomachache), পেট ভরেছে (I'm full — literally “stomach has filled”).

**In Bengal the pharmacy is often the first stop, not the doctor.** A ফার্মাসিস্ট can usually read simple symptoms and hand out medicine without a prescription. ⚠️ Handy, but for a fever lasting over two days, a rash, or unclear pain, ask to be referred: **ডাক্তার দেখানো দরকার?** (do I need to see a doctor?). And keep the names of drugs you're allergic to written down — brand names can differ.

grammars.title: The -কে ending and “have to”

head: “Have to” sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: The medicine has to be taken.

after: **For the past, change হবে to হয়েছিল or হল:** আমাকে যেতে হয়েছিল (I had to go). For a repeated present, use **হয়**: রোজ ওষুধ খেতে হয় (I have to take medicine every day).

grammars.title: The body and complaints
after: ⚠️ **গলা means throat, neck, and also voice.** গলা ব্যথা is a sore throat; গলা বসে গেছে means “my voice is hoarse”. Say গলা ব্যথা to a tea seller and he'll offer you **আদা চা** at once — ginger tea, the home remedy all of Bengal trusts.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Four practical health tips for Bengal
items: **Drinking water.** In many places tap water isn't for drinking. Phrases you need: **বোতলের পানি দিন** (bottled water, please) or **ফোটানো পানি?** (boiled water?). Avoid ice at roadside stalls in your first weeks.

**Heat and dehydration.** Bengali summers are humid and fierce. **স্যালাইন** *sêalain* — oral rehydration salts — is sold at every pharmacy for a few taka, and locals drink it as a habit, not as an emergency remedy.
**Mosquitoes.** ডেঙ্গু (dengue fever) is real in the rainy season. Words you need: **মশা** *môsha* (mosquito), **মশারি** *môshari* (mosquito net), **কয়েল** *kôyél* (mosquito coil).

**Home remedies you'll be offered:** আদা চা (ginger tea) for the throat, গরম পানি (warm water) for almost everything, and মধু (honey) for a cough. Accepting them is accepting care, not just treatment.

blocks.text: A note on how Bengalis respond to news that you're ill. Say you're not feeling well, and the reaction is likely not brief sympathy but **a series of actions**: someone will take your temperature, someone else will cook something, and another will walk you to the pharmacy. Refusing it all with “please don't trouble yourselves” will actually hurt. Accept at least one, and say **আপনারা অনেক করলেন** — “you've done so much”.

items: I've had a fever for two days.

answers: আমাকে যেতে হবে। — আপনাকে বিশ্রাম নিতে হবে। — আমাকে ওষুধ খেতে হবে। — তাকে ডাক্তার দেখাতে হবে।
আমার গলা ব্যথা করছে। — আমার জ্বর হয়েছে। — ওষুধ খাবারের পরে খেতে হবে। — হাসপাতাল কোথায়? — আমাকে একটু সাহায্য করুন।
আমার মাথা ব্যথা করছে। — দুই দিন ধরে আমার জ্বর হয়েছে। — খাবারের পরে ওষুধ খেতে হবে। — আমাকে ডাক্তারের কাছে যেতে হবে। — আমাকে একটু সাহায্য করুন। — আমার শরীর ভালো নেই।
